The budget phone has quietly moved up a price bracket. Several models on this list cost noticeably more today than when they first went on sale earlier this year, and phones that once sat around Rs 15,000 now ask for something closer to Rs 25,000. What that extra money buys has shifted too. Batteries of 6,000mAh and above are now the norm, high refresh-rate screens are standard, and IP ratings that used to belong to pricier phones show up on handsets well under Rs 30,000. Cameras have barely moved. The seven phones below cover the range, from a no-frills 4G Samsung to performance-led picks from OnePlus and Vivo.The Nord CE6 Lite runs on MediaTek's Dimensity 7400 Apex chip, backed by a 5,300 sq mm vapour chamber, and drives a 6.72-inch Full HD+ LCD at up to 144Hz. The 7,000mAh battery charges at 45W and supports bypass charging, which keeps heat in check during long gaming sessions. OnePlus has trimmed elsewhere to get here: the screen is LCD rather than AMOLED, the fingerprint sensor sits on the side, and the phone is rated IP64. It runs OxygenOS 16, with five years of software support promised.The Galaxy A07 5G is built for people who keep a phone for years. Samsung promises six Android OS updates, which is rare at this end of the market, and the 6,000mAh battery with 25W charging suits that kind of long ownership.The 6.7-inch HD+ LCD runs at 120Hz, and the MediaTek Dimensity 6300 handles calls, UPI, social apps and light games comfortably. A 50MP main camera is paired with a 2MP depth sensor, while Samsung Wallet and Auto Blocker, which stops unauthorised app installs, round out a phone that is more about peace of mind than speed.The Galaxy M08 is the most affordable phone here and the only one that skips 5G altogether. Inside is the MediaTek Helio G99+, a dependable 4G chip, driving a 6.7-inch HD+ LCD at 90Hz. There is a 6,000mAh battery, a 50MP main camera and an 8MP selfie camera. It makes sense for someone whose day revolves around WhatsApp, YouTube and payments, or as a second phone, as long as 5G is not on the list.The Galaxy M17e 5G shares most of its hardware with the A07 5G: the same Dimensity 6300 chip, the same 6.7-inch HD+ 120Hz LCD, the same 50MP + 2MP camera pair and the same 6,000mAh battery with 25W charging. It is rated IP54 for dust and splashes, and Samsung's six-generation OS promise carries over, along with Gemini Live and Circle to Search. The real difference is price. The M17e costs Rs 2,500 less for the same 6GB + 128GB configuration.The Galaxy F07 pairs a 6.7-inch HD+ LCD at 90Hz with a 50MP main camera, an 8MP selfie camera and a 5,000mAh battery with 25W charging, and it carries an IP54 rating. The 4GB + 64GB configuration is the tight spot. 64GB fills up quickly once WhatsApp media and a couple of games settle in, so the microSD slot will see use.The Vivo T5X's Dimensity 7400 Turbo puts it in the same performance bracket as the Nord CE6 Lite, and the 7,200mAh battery with 44W charging is the largest here. Vivo has also gone hard on durability, with IP68 and IP69 ratings alongside MIL-STD-810H certification. The 6.76-inch Full HD+ LCD runs at 120Hz, the 50MP Sony IMX852 main camera records 4K video, and there is a 32MP selfie camera and stereo speakers. The trade-off is weight, at 219g. Software is OriginOS 6 on Android 16.The Oppo K14 5G leans on stamina and toughness rather than speed. Its 7,000mAh battery charges at 45W and supports reverse wired charging, so it can top up a pair of earbuds or another phone, and IP66, IP68 and IP69 ratings sit alongside MIL-STD-810H certification. The 6.75-inch HD+ LCD runs at 120Hz, reaches up to 1,125 nits and works with wet hands. Under the hood is the Dimensity 6300 chip. The 50MP main camera comes with AI editing tools such as AI Eraser.
Article Summary: The Nord CE6 Lite runs on MediaTek's Dimensity 7400 Apex chip, backed by a 5,300 sq mm vapour chamber, and drives a 6.72-inch Full HD+ LCD at up to 144Hz. There is a 6,000mAh battery, a 50MP camera and an 8MP selfie camera. The Galaxy A07 5G is built for people who keep a phone for years. It makes sense for someone whose day revolves around YouTube, WhatsApp and payments.

Palo Alto Networks CEO Nikesh Arora has spoken on the recent global outages that disrupted everyday essentials. He pointed to a warning the industry gave businesses six months ago. According to Arora, artificial intelligence (AI) is making it much easier for hackers to launch large-scale cyberattacks, letting them hit multiple customers and systems faster than ever before. His comments come right after a rough week for US tech infrastructure. Widespread outages disrupted major technology platforms, banks, and airline operations. Users ran into trouble trying to access popular services like iCloud, Apple Pay, Gmail, and Google Search. These glitches added to a broader wave of recent disruptions that have also hit Microsoft services and aviation systems.," Arora said.Interestingly, Arora pointed out that hackers are not the only reason systems are crashing.In a rush to stay safe, software vendors are finding security flaws and pushing out fixes as fast as they can. While those updates are well-intentioned, they are creating a massive headache for the people who keep company networks running.Arora explained that Chief Information Officers (CIOs) and IT teams are currently “overwhelmed with goodness.” Because they are being flooded with so many updates at once, some of the recent global outages are actually a direct result of that heavy wave of patching.” he said.As traditional security teams struggle to keep up with the speed of modern threats, Arora is urging companies to rethink their defenses before an attack hits. To avoid getting caught off guard, he recommends companies take a few immediate steps:Arora also stressed that patching together quick, reactive fixes across different systems is no longer a workable plan. Instead, companies need to overhaul their Security Operations Centers (SOC) so they can spot and stop threats in record time.

Article Title: As Anthropic's IPO is less than 24 hours away, here's Blackstone's 'junk warning' to investors
Article Text:
Anthropic’s leaked IPO filing reveals soaring revenue, massive infrastructure costs, customer concentration and the financial risks behind its AI ambitions.

What a junk rating could mean for Anthropic

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Where Blackstone has money at stake

Anthropic is expected to go public on November 19. The Claude maker plans to list on Nasdaq under the ticker ANT. Its latest US filing sets an expected price range of $70 to $78 a share, putting the total offering at about $61 billion at the midpoint. However, Blackstone has reportedly warned its investors about buying shares of the AI companyA Financial Times report citing people familiar with the matter claims Blackstone has told its investors that Anthropic could receive a “high” junk credit rating after its IPO due to the AI company’s $63 billion chip financing deal. The private capital firm had previously expected Anthropic to reach investment grade by year-end. A rating in the BB range would put Anthropic near the top of the speculative-grade category and could make it more expensive to borrow for computing infrastructure.A below-investment-grade rating could narrow Anthropic’s pool of lenders. Some insurers and pension funds face limits on how much lower-rated debt they can hold, and lenders generally demand higher yields from borrowers they consider riskier. The FT reported that Anthropic outlined plans to spend more than $800 billion on computing infrastructure through 2045.The rating also matters for Anthropic’s existing credit facility. Its offering documents say the company can elect to have guarantees and collateral released if it obtains investment-grade ratings from at least two of Moody’s, S&P and Fitch and meets other conditions. FT noted that none of those three agencies had issued a rating for Anthropic when its report was released last month.The chip financing, known as Project North Star, lets Anthropic lease 1.5 gigawatts of Google-designed chips. Broadcom, which co-develops the chips and has an investment-grade rating, guarantees more than $42 billion of senior loans.Another $18 billion in junior debt is backed by Anthropic’s lease payments and ranks behind the senior loans for repayment in a default. Blackstone’s funds invested $9 billion in the junior debt at a yield above 10%, the FT reported.
Article Summary: Anthropic is expected to go public on November 19. The AI maker plans to list on Nasdaq under the ticker ANT. Its latest US filing sets an expected price range of $70 to $78 a share. Blackstone has reportedly warned its investors about buying shares of the AI company.

Article Text:
Sharp contrast with Jensen Huang’s stance

China sales come to an end: Colette Kress, Nvidia CEO

Nvidia board focuses on national security

Microsoft remains committed to Nvidia partnership

Nvidia’s approach to China appears to be undergoing a significant change after the departure of founder Jensen Huang, who had spent years lobbying for greater access to the Chinese market. According to a report by Bloomberg, Nvidia’s interim CEO Colette Kress has said that the company is no longer shipping licensed Hopper datacenter chips to China and does not expect such sales to contribute to future results. Speaking during the latest earnings call of the company, Kress stated that the AI chip giant sold around $2.4 billion worth of licensed Hopper datacenter products in China during the third quarter. However, she added that the company’s future guidance does not include any licensed Hopper datacenter products and also confirmed that Nvidia has stopped shipping those products to Chinese customers.This move of Nvidia marks a notable departure from the position championed by Jensen Huang, who had repeatedly argued for maintaining access to the Chinese market and sought US government approval to sell advanced AI processors there.As per the Bloomberg report, Nvidia earlier pushed Washington for permission to sell its Blackwell AI chips to China. While, the Trump administration did not approve those requests, it later permitted the sales of Hopper-based H200 processors, which are older than Nvidia's latest Rubin-generation products. For the uninitiated, Huang has been one of the most vocal advocates for exports to China, frequently emphasising the importance of the market to Nvidia’s long-term growth strategy.Nvidia’s interim CEO Colette Kress has not explained the reason as to why the company is ending shipments to China, but her comments does indicate that Nvidia is stepping away from a business that generated billions of dollars in recent revenue. The announcement also comes at a time when the US government tightens restrictions on advanced AI chip exports. Recently, the Trump administration also introduced measures which are directed towards increasing scrutiny of processor exports and limiting sales to overseas data centers that could offer Chinese companies with remote access to advanced AI infrastructure.The report also adds that the shift in Nvidia’s stance also reflects growing concerns around national security and export controls. Harvey Jones, who was appointed Nvidia's first board chair last week, said the company recognises that changing national security dynamics are having a major impact on the market. "The company's next CEO will need to navigate those waters very carefully," Jones said, according to Bloomberg.Nvidia also announced the creation of a dedicated board-level committee focused on national security and export-control issues, signalling that geopolitical considerations are likely to play a larger role in future business decisions.Despite Nvidia's leadership turmoil, Nadella expressed confidence in the company's management team and long-term prospects. "Nvidia does have a lot of human capital and very capable leadership," he said, highlighting interim CEO and Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress, who previously worked at Microsoft.Nadella also stressed the importance of Microsoft's ongoing relationship with the chipmaker, noting that the company is continuing to scale deployment of Nvidia's next-generation Vera Rubin processors. "I'm making sure that we have the same type of partnership, and we're scaling Rubins as we speak," Nadella said. "It's a pretty critical project for us."Microsoft is one of Nvidia's largest customers, purchasing vast quantities of AI accelerators for its cloud infrastructure. The two companies have maintained a close partnership during the AI boom, with Nadella and Huang frequently appearing together at industry events.
Article Summary: N Nvidia is no longer shipping licensed Hopper datacenter chips to China. Colette Kress, interim CEO, said the company does not expect such sales to contribute to future results. This marks a notable departure from the position championed by Jensen Huang, who had repeatedly argued for maintaining access to the Chinese market. The shift in Nvidia’s stance also reflects growing concerns around national security and export controls.

Article Title: US expands 'China ban' on Nvidia chips to 12 other countries: Here's the full list and what it means
Article Text:
' China ban ' on Nvidia chips: What the new restrictions mean

Five countries named

Exemptions

Markets react; Nvidia shares fall

Pressure on Commerce Department grows

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Countries affected by the proposed rule

The US Commerce Department has now unveiled new restrictions aimed at preventing Chinese companies and other US adversaries from accessing advanced artificial intelligence computing power through overseas data centers, according to Bloomberg report. Under an interim rule release on November 16, the datacenter operators in counties including Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil will be required to obtain a US government licence before purchasing advanced AI chips from manufacturers such as Nvidia. The measure is designed to prevent companies from bypassing existing export controls through remote access to computing infrastructure located outside China.“The rule is designed to ensure that existing restrictions on access to sensitive American technology cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries,” the Commerce Department said in a statement.This move of the US Commerce Department highlights the growing US concerns that advanced cloud-computing networks have made it easier for Chinese entities to remotely tap into powerful AI systems powered by US-designed semiconductors, even when they cannot directly import the chips themselves.By extending licensing requirements to a wider group of countries, Washington is seeking to align rules governing remote access with existing restrictions on the physical shipment of advanced AI hardware. Under the proposal, licence applications will be reviewed on a case-by-case basis.The rule requires licences to export, re-export or transfer advanced semiconductors to Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore or Thailand. Licences will be considered case by case, and the rule describes these countries as presenting a “higher-than-normal risk of diversion.” The department said the rule is meant to ensure that existing restrictions on sensitive American technology “cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries. ”The rule exempts US-headquartered companies operating in the listed countries, which can keep shipping AI chips there without a licence. It also exempts shipments to data centers used as commercial recommender systems for online retailers or social media companies. The draft rule takes effect once it is published in the Federal Register, which had not happened as of 9 am Monday, Bloomberg reported.Nvidia shares fell as much as 2.9% on the news, while the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index dropped as much as 5.5%. The restrictions apply not only to Nvidia but also to other US companies that manufacture advanced AI processors.The draft rule arrives amid heightened scrutiny of US export-control enforcement following allegations involving Nvidia and Singapore-based Megaspeed International. According to the Bloomberg report, the Commerce Department and senior officials, including Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, have faced increasing criticism over their handling of export-control programmes. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent recently suggested that the Commerce Department had not acted quickly enough to tighten restrictions."As I said, many other departments were pushing for this, and Commerce had the pen," Bessent said during an appearance on Fox News' Sunday Morning Futures, according to Bloomberg. The Commerce Department's statement announcing the new rule said it was written "by and at the direction" of the Treasury Department and the National Security Council, indicating broad support within the administration for tougher controls.According to the Bloomberg report, the new licensing requirements would apply to data-centre operators in 12 countries:* Singapore* Malaysia* Thailand* Indonesia* Brazil* Mexico* Philippines* Vietnam* India* South Africa* Saudi Arabia* United Arab EmiratesThe countries listed above have become an important hub for AI infrastructure, cloud-computing facilities and semiconductor-related investments. These are the reasons why US is making them a focal point in order to control the access of advanced AI technologies.
Article Summary: New restrictions aimed at preventing Chinese companies from accessing advanced artificial intelligence computing power through overseas data centers. Datacenter operators in counties including Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil will be required to obtain a US government licence. The measure is designed to prevent companies from bypassing existing export controls through remote access.

Article Title: Canada faces pushback from Meta, Apple, Alphabet and Signal over Canadian bill that could force them to weaken encryption
Article Text:
Why tech companies are threatening to leave Canada

The ‘fight’ over encryption and ‘backdoors’

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Prime Minister Mark Carney’s government is reportedly running into fierce resistance from major technology companies over proposed security legislation that would force digital platforms to retain and hand over user data to law enforcement. Executives and lobbyists from Facebook-parent Meta, Apple , and Google-parent Alphabet said to be leading a last-ditch push in Ottawa to rewrite the legislation before it becomes law. Leaders from Meta, Signal Messenger and Tailscale are set to take their objections directly to a key Canadian Senate committee hearing that will shape the bill’s final text, Bloomberg reported.Known as Bill C-22, the “lawful access” legislation is designed to let Canada’s police services and spy agency require electronic service providers to preserve and turn over specific metadata. While the Canadian government argues the rules simply bring the country in line with its Five Eyes and Group of Seven (G7) allies, tech companies, privacy advocates, and US lawmakers contend the bill goes much further – putting user privacy and platform security at risk.Meta has warned that the legislation would effectively turn its platforms into “an arm of the government’s surveillance apparatus.” “There’s a real possibility that both the security and the privacy of Canadian users of these systems is really undermined,” Rachel Curran, Meta’s head of public policy in Canada, said in an interview, the publication reported.For Carney’s government, the standoff carries real economic and diplomatic risks, including chilling tech investment, straining relations with the US and pushing privacy-focused services out of the country altogether. Signal has threatened to pull out of the Canadian market if Bill C-22 passes in its current form while Proton AG, a Swiss tech firm, has said it would reconsider its expansion plans in Canada.Critics take particular issue with a provision allowing authorities to force service providers to store certain user metadata for up to six months in case law enforcement requests it.Bill C-22 could also require certain companies to unlock encrypted data – though only if the company built the encryption itself and holds the keys needed to unlock it. Earlier this year, lawmakers amended the bill to clarify that firms cannot be forced to introduce a “systemic vulnerability” into their software.Those safeguards were meant to reassure companies like Signal and Meta (which owns WhatsApp) that end-to-end encryption wouldn’t be targeted. Because end-to-end encryption ensures only the sender and recipient can read a message, the companies themselves have no way to decrypt the content.Still, privacy groups and tech leaders argue the bill leaves the government with broad authority to order firms to build “technical capabilities” to intercept communications and hand over data. Tech companies have consistently maintained that they cannot build a law enforcement “backdoor” without weakening security for everyone.Curran called any order that weakens Meta’s systems a “red line” for the company and likely its peers. “It probably puts Canada in a position where there’s going to eventually be a bit of a standoff between service providers and the government, and it’s not good for Canadians,” she added.Meanwhile, Canada’s public safety minister Gary Anandasangaree has maintained that Bill C-22 was already revised to address the encryption concerns, accusing Big Tech critics of spreading misinformation.“Bill C-22 does not authorise indiscriminate surveillance and does not permit or compel companies to introduce systemic vulnerabilities or so-called ‘backdoors.’ Any claims suggesting otherwise are incorrect,” said Simon Lafortune, the minister’s spokesperson, in a statement.Apple has acknowledged the government’s efforts to improve the draft, but said the current bill would still hurt its ability to protect users with encryption and privacy tools, “even as AI and other evolving technologies provide hackers with new tools to exploit cybersecurity weaknesses.”
Article Summary: Canadian government running into fierce resistance over proposed security legislation. Bill C-22 would force digital platforms to retain and hand over user data to law enforcement. Meta, Signal Messenger and Tailscale are set to take their objections directly to a key Canadian Senate committee hearing that will shape the bill’s final text.

Article Title: US government's Department of Commerce and Department of Justice ‘break rule’, issue joint statement on MegaSpeed, the company at 'centre' of Nvidia founder Jensen Huang's 'romantic scandal'
Article Text:
Department of Commerce and the Department of Justice's joint statement on investigation into Singaporean company Megaspeed

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

For the first time, two US government departments -- US Department of Commerce and Department of Justice -- have issued a joint statement on MegaSpeed, the Singapore-based company caught in Nvidia founder Jensen Huang's scandal. The statement makes it clear what made the two departments break the rule of not commenting on and ongoing investigations. The statement says, "While we don’t typically comment on ongoing investigations, it is in the public interest to provide the facts and address inaccurate information circulating in public reporting."For those unaware, the Singapore-based cloud computing company MegaSpeed has faced heightened scrutiny since former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said that he had been unfaithful to his wife following reports linking him to former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang. Huang resigned as CEO of Nvidia on November 12 amid fallout from reports about his extramarital relationships, one of which was reportedly a direct reportee.On its website, Megaspeed describes itself as a "core business partner" of Nvidia’s computing power cloud business in the region. It enables customers to rent computing power from Nvidia GPUs. The company has offices in Singapore and Indonesia.The Department of Commerce and the Department of Justice are providing the public with an update on the investigation of the Singaporean company Megaspeed, which has attracted significant public attention in the last week.While we don’t typically comment on ongoing investigations, it is in the public interest to provide the facts and address inaccurate information circulating in public reporting.After identifying suspicious activity through proactive monitoring of potential sensitive semiconductor diversion, the Department of Commerce initiated an investigation into Megaspeed in 2024 for potential export control violations. In May 2025, Department of Commerce investigators requested records from Nvidia concerning direct or indirect sales to Megaspeed. In June 2025, Nvidia placed Megaspeed on its “no sell” list. Based on the Department of Commerce’s investigation, agents from the Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security, in conjunction with Singaporean law enforcement officials, conducted an on-site, in-person, end-use check at Megaspeed in June 2025 and interviewed CEO Alice Huang.Following this enforcement action, the Department of Justice took the lead role in the criminal investigation of Megaspeed.The Department of Justice and the Department of Commerce’s Bureau of Industry and Security working together will bring the full extent of the law against Megaspeed for any criminal conduct that may have occurred. This investigation is the result of the excellent work of the Department of Commerce under Secretary Howard Lutnick and the law enforcement efforts of the Department of Justice under Attorney General Todd Blanche.The Department of Justice and the Department of Commerce have an extremely strong track record of bringing semiconductor smugglers to justice. Under the Trump Administration, seventeen defendants across six separate investigations have been charged in connection with allegations of smuggling billions of dollars’ worth of semiconductors. Furthermore, the Department of Commerce has brought monetary penalties to new highs across export control cases, representing an eighteen-fold increase over the Biden administration.Sensitive technologies like semiconductors are among the most valuable and strategic assets of the U.S. economy, and the Department of Justice and the Department of Commerce will remain vigilant in pursuing justice for those who want to compromise America’s technological edge.
Article Summary: US Department of Commerce and Department of Justice have issued a joint statement on MegaSpeed, the Singapore-based company caught in Nvidia founder Jensen Huang's scandal. The statement says, "While we don’t typically comment on ongoing investigations, it is in the public interest to provide the facts"

Article Title: EY India opens registrations for sixth Board Effectiveness programme with focus on AI, cybersecurity
Article Text:
Boards expected to play a bigger strategic role

Focus on governance, technology and risk oversight

More than 40 hours of learning

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Wider leadership participation

EY India has announced the sixth cohort of its Executive Program on Board Effectiveness, aimed at equipping current directors and senior executives with the skills needed to navigate evolving boardroom responsibilities, including oversight of artificial intelligence (AI), cybersecurity and corporate governance. The four-week programme will commence on 19 November 2026 and is designed for existing board members as well as senior leaders aspiring to take up board positions. According to EY India, the initiative seeks to strengthen participants' strategic judgment, financial oversight and governance capabilities as expectations from corporate boards continue to expand beyond traditional compliance functions.EY India highlighted that directors are increasingly expected to contribute to strategy formation, risk governance, technology oversight, financial resilience and long-term value creation, rather than serving solely as compliance watchdogs. The firm cited findings from the ISB Corporate Governance Report 2025, which surveyed more than 200 directors from BSE 500 companies. While 98% of respondents said their boards were compliant with governance requirements, only 17% reported that their boards actively shaped company strategy. A further 36% said their boards had limited or no involvement beyond reviewing management plans.Commenting on the programme, Aashish Kasad, Partner and India Region Diversity & Inclusiveness Business Sponsor at EY India, said the transition from executive leadership to the boardroom requires a shift from operating a business to challenging, guiding and overseeing it."Directors need to connect strategy with financial resilience, governance and deliberate on organisation readiness on topical matters such as impact of AI and cybersecurity, while exercising independent judgment," Kasad said, adding that the programme is intended to help leaders contribute to boards with greater clarity and confidence.The Executive Program on Board Effectiveness includes more than 40 hours of learning across nine sessions. Topics covered include board leadership and effectiveness, directors' responsibilities, board committees, environmental, social and governance (ESG) issues, financial statement interpretation, AI and cybersecurity, board recruitment and emerging governance challenges. Participants will also engage in governance case studies, simulated board and committee discussions, and scenario-based exercises designed to enhance strategic contribution, risk awareness, stakeholder stewardship, integrity and ethical decision-making.Originally introduced as a platform for senior women leaders, the programme has now been expanded to a broader leadership audience. EY India said it plans to offer two cohorts each year, enabling more professionals to prepare for boardroom responsibilities and benefit from peer learning opportunities. The programme is targeted at CXO-level executives seeking board positions, senior leaders from corporate, public and non-profit organisations, investor representatives serving on boards, leaders from multinational companies and Indian subsidiaries, as well as existing directors looking to strengthen their effectiveness in a rapidly changing governance environment.
Article Summary: EY India has announced the sixth cohort of its Executive Program on Board Effectiveness. The four-week programme will commence on 19 November 2026 and is designed for existing board members as well as senior leaders aspiring to take up board positions. EY India said it plans to offer two cohorts each year, enabling more professionals to prepare for boardroom responsibilities.

Article Title: Microsoft 365 outage: Company blames a 'triple' failure for 24-hour-plus global Outlook disruption; Microsoft EVP Charles Lamanna says: Three main factors that...
Article Text:
Microsoft explains its global outage

A July bug slipped past Microsoft 365's load testing

A Teams failover and 14% missing capacity exposed the bug

Outlook stayed down longest because Exchange Online could not switch gateways

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Microsoft has explained what disrupted Outlook, Exchange Online and a string of other Microsoft 365 services for more than 24 hours last week, and the answer is not one fault but three. A software bug that had sat unnoticed on its servers since July, a sudden rise in traffic and a chunk of server capacity already offline all lined up on November 12. The result was a chain reaction that left more than 80% of the servers behind a key Microsoft 365 networking gateway unresponsive at the worst point.Charles Lamanna, Microsoft's executive vice president for Copilot, Agents and Platform, detailed the root cause of the Microsoft 365 outage in a post on X on Monday. "The incident on Thursday, November 12th, 2026, was caused by three main factors that together caused a global outage for the networking gateway that fronts many Microsoft 365 services," he wrote. He also apologised: "We are deeply sorry for the impact to all our customers and recognize the impact that this has on their normal business & operations. "The first factor was a latent defect. Under certain load conditions, lock contention inside an internal process left servers overwhelmed and unresponsive.The bug came from a fix built specifically for Microsoft 365 networking gateway servers. Lamanna said neither the defect nor that fix applies to broader Windows deployments.The change began rolling out in July, cleared safe deployment, reached servers worldwide over several weeks and ran for more than three months without trouble.So why did testing miss it? Microsoft's load tests leaned on its weaker hardware with fewer cores, while the contention problem gets worse on newer machines with more cores. The test labs' traffic and hardware mix did not match the live fleet.Microsoft runs two independent network gateway systems inside Microsoft 365, so services can move between them during disruptions. About 15 hours before the outage, Teams failed over from the alternative gateway to the "primary" one, which also handles Exchange Online. The company calls this routine, but it added load and changed traffic patterns on that gateway.At the same time, nearly 14% of the gateway's server capacity was out of service because of an unrelated issue from the day before. That alone caused no harm, since the service had enough headroom.Together, though, the extra load and thinner capacity triggered the July bug during peak US traffic hours. Requests piled up until servers stopped responding. Microsoft's traffic management then moved users to healthy endpoints, as designed, which simply spread the same load across fewer machines. In under two hours, the defect had hit servers across the fleet.A separate issue meant the bulkheads between regional "capacity units" also failed to contain the damage, letting a gateway problem become a global outage.Teams, OneDrive, SharePoint and Office apps could move off the faulty infrastructure, which is why they came back sooner. Teams chats and meetings worked for most of the outage. Exchange Online, which powers Outlook email, could not make that switch.Recovery was a fight of its own. Servers returning to service were flooded by queued traffic and went down again. Microsoft's automated recovery systems were not designed for such a broad failure, and because the bug was months old, the usual rollback, flighting and feature flag tools could not quickly reverse it. Even the company's status updates during the outage said it had "not identified any recent change correlated with the start of impact.Engineers eventually built an update that returned the code path to its last known good state. They then pulled groups of servers out of service, applied the fix and restarted them, in some cases more than half a region at a time.Microsoft first flagged the problem at 11:24 pm IST on November 12, for users in the Americas, before it spread to at least 70 countries and hit Copilot, government offices, courts and hospitals. In India, IndiGo and Akasa Air reported problems with their customer-support email systems, while OpenAI and Anthropic flagged issues with their Microsoft 365 integrations. The Microsoft executive had already ruled out foul play on November 13, writing, "This was not a cyberattack or an issue caused by AI tooling. "A final Post-Incident Review (PIR) is due later this week. It should also shed light on the separate issue that let the failure jump across regions, which Monday's summary leaves unexplained.
Article Summary: Microsoft 365 went down for more than 24 hours on November 12. A software bug that had sat unnoticed on its servers since July, a sudden rise in traffic and a chunk of server capacity already offline all lined up. The result was a chain reaction that left more than 80% of the servers behind a key Microsoft 365 networking gateway unresponsive.

Article Title: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani has an update on 'house tax' that reportedly made Google founder Sergey Brin exit city
Article Text:
NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani

Here’s the update on ‘house tax’ that Zohran Mamdani shared

What is Mamdani’s pied-à-terre tax and which properties are covered

Why Sergey Brin 'exited' New York City

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani recently shared an update on the pied-à-terre surcharge, popularly called as 'house tax'. In a post on X (formerly Twitter), Zohran Mamdani said that the city has billed over $500 million to rich owners of second homes. “That’s half a billion dollars to invest in a City that works for all New Yorkers,” Mamdani wrote. Introduced earlier this year, the pied-à-terre tax apples to homes worth over $5 million that are not the owner’s main residence. Among those impacted by the tax includes Google founder Sergey Brin , Amazon founder Jeff Bezos and Dell CEO Michael Dell. A Bloomberg report in July said that Sergey Brin walked away from a sizable bet on New York City apartment, selling his stake in a struggling real estate fund for just six cents on the dollar.Sharing the X post, Zohran Mamdani wrote:“An update on our pied-à-terre surcharge: We’ve billed more than $500 million to owners of second homes worth more than $5 million. That’s half a billion dollars to invest in a City that works for all New Yorkers”.As mentioned above, the new pied-à-terre tax is a surcharge on houses that are not the primary residence of owners. It applies to one-, two- and three-family homes valued at more than $5 million, as well as condominiums and co-ops valued at $1 million or more, if those properties are not a person's primary residence.The measure is intended primarily to cover owners who maintain homes in New York City while living elsewhere for most of the year and therefore do not pay New York City income taxes.According to a Bloomberg report, Google founder Sergey Brin offloaded his sizable holding in a New York City apartment back to the fund's manager, A&E Real Estate. Amphitheatre LLC, an entity tied to Brin, sold its shares in a fund holding nearly 5,900 units across Manhattan, Brooklyn, Queens and the Bronx, the report stated. Many of those apartments fall under New York's rent-stabilization program.A&E then confirmed the buyout without naming Brin, saying the investor "was willing to accept six cents on the dollar on their original equity investment to divest itself from the New York City multifamily sector.”
Article Summary: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani recently shared an update on the pied-à-terre surcharge, popularly called as 'house tax' In a post on X (formerly Twitter), Zoh Ran M amdani said that the city has billed over $500 million to rich owners of second homes. “That’s half a billion dollars to invest in a City that works for all New Yorkers,” Mamdari wrote.

Article Title: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella praises Jensen Huang, but makes it clear: It is not up to me to ...
Article Text:
Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella

Jensen Huang says he is opening to returning to Nvidia as CEO

Microsoft remains committed to Nvidia partnership

Data centre growth depends on community trust

AI helped Microsoft recover from outage

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Buyout programme gives employees more choice

Poll Vote & Share your view Do you think Jensen Huang should return as CEO of Nvidia? Yes No Unsure 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella has expressed his admiration for former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang after his departure from the AI chip giant, but he also made it clear that any decision about the return of Huang is not his to make. According to a report Fortune, speaking at a media roundtable during Microsoft’s Ignite conference in San Francisco, Nadella described Huang as ‘a singular person’ who has made some significant contributions to both Nvidia and the broader technology industry. However, he stopped short of endorsing a potential comeback for the Nvidia co-founder. "I just want to give him space for what he needs to do there, and it's not up to me. It's up to the Nvidia board to decide what happens next," Nadella said. He added that he has "all the admiration, respect for what Jensen has done for this industry, and what he's done for Nvidia," noting that the two have worked together for many years.Huang stepped down as Nvidia CEO last week amid controversy surrounding revelations about his personal life. The long-time executive, who co-founded Nvidia more than three decades ago and helped transform it into the world's leading AI chipmaker, later said he would be willing to return as CEO if given the opportunity.However, Nvidia board chair Harvey Jones subsequently indicated that the company had no plans to bring Huang back to the top role, leaving uncertainty around the executive's future.Despite Nvidia's leadership turmoil, Nadella expressed confidence in the company's management team and long-term prospects. "Nvidia does have a lot of human capital and very capable leadership," he said, highlighting interim CEO and Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress, who previously worked at Microsoft.Nadella also stressed the importance of Microsoft's ongoing relationship with the chipmaker, noting that the company is continuing to scale deployment of Nvidia's next-generation Vera Rubin processors. "I'm making sure that we have the same type of partnership, and we're scaling Rubins as we speak," Nadella said. "It's a pretty critical project for us."Microsoft is one of Nvidia's largest customers, purchasing vast quantities of AI accelerators for its cloud infrastructure. The two companies have maintained a close partnership during the AI boom, with Nadella and Huang frequently appearing together at industry events.During the discussion, Nadella also commented on growing opposition to data centre developments across parts of the United States. He said technology companies must earn public trust by demonstrating tangible local benefits rather than relying on lobbying efforts in Washington. According to Nadella, concerns around electricity usage, infrastructure strain and local disruption can only be addressed through long-term engagement with communities."I don't think the public is getting it wrong," he said, adding that Microsoft's data centre expansion plans remain unchanged despite recent political developments.Nadella noted that the biggest constraints on data centre construction continue to be power availability, chip production capacity and memory supply rather than election outcomes.The Microsoft chief also addressed the massive Microsoft Outlook outage last week. The service disruption impacted the functioning of Teams, Copilot, SharePoint and other Microsoft 365 services. Nadella emphasised that the service disruption was not caused by any AI-generate code other AI deployments. Instead, he said that it was a ‘perfect story’ in which a software bug emerged during routine testing under specific web traffic conditions.He further stated that the internal tools at Microsoft actually helped the engineers to diagnose the issue and then resolve the problem.Apart from Huang, Nadella also talked about the recent voluntary buyout offer of Microsoft which was extended to almost 60,000 employees. As per the Microsoft CEO, the programme was aimed to offer more control to the workers over their career decisions instead of leaving them uncertain about the future when it comes to organisational changes. "There are some teams that are changing faster, some teams that are in a different place," Nadella said, referring to the varying pace of transformation across different parts of Microsoft.
Article Summary: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella has expressed his admiration for former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. Huang stepped down as Nvidia CEO last week amid controversy surrounding revelations about his personal life. Nvidia board chair Harvey Jones subsequently indicated that the company had no plans to bring Huang back to the top role.

Article Title: Apple revamps Maps in India with street views, speed limits, and local-language labels
Article Text:
Apple rolls out all-new map across India

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Finding the right turn in India often means looking for a petrol pump or a flyover pillar rather than a street sign. Apple is bringing those familiar cues to Maps, rolling out a rebuilt India map with landmark-based directions, street-level imagery and labels in English and local languages.The update announced on Wednesday gives Apple a stronger offering in a market where finding the right turn can involve distinguishing a service lane from a flyover or locating an entrance on an unnamed road. Winning regular users, however, will depend on how reliably it handles those everyday journeys.Apple has expanded its conversational navigation instructions in India to refer to petrol pumps, pillars and other recognisable points along a route. Lane guidance is intended to help drivers position themselves before a turn or an elevated road. Users can also plan journeys with up to 15 stops.The company said the rebuilt map offers more accurate navigation and greater detail on roads, buildings, parks and shopping centres. It did not provide comparative accuracy figures or explain how frequently road changes would be incorporated.“We’ve also designed the map for India’s specific navigation needs, including enhanced Natural Language Guidance and customised dual-language labels,” said Max Muller, Apple’s vice-president of Apple Maps.Labels combine the device’s language with the local language of the area being viewed. Someone using an English-language iPhone would see Hindi alongside English in Delhi and Marathi alongside English in Mumbai. Apple said Maps now supports 11 languages used in India.Look Around, Apple’s interactive street-level imagery feature, is also arriving in India, alongside more than 300 three-dimensional landmarks. Augmented-reality walking directions allow users to scan nearby buildings with an iPhone to establish their position and see instructions overlaid on their surroundings.Public transport directions cover Ahmedabad, Bengaluru, Chennai, Delhi, Hyderabad, Kolkata, Mumbai and Pune, as well as Indian Railways. Travellers can find stations, save routes and receive alerts when they need to get off.Drivers can report accidents, hazards and speed checks through Siri, while arrival-time sharing updates friends or family if a journey is significantly delayed. Charging stops can be incorporated into routes for certain compatible electric vehicles, although the announcement did not identify supported models in India.Cycling directions, custom routes and previews of frequently taken commutes round out the update. Apple said commute learning happens on the device.The overhaul puts Apple up against Google Maps, the default navigation choice for many Indians, including iPhone users. Getting them to switch will require more than sharper imagery: Apple will have to match the everyday usefulness of Google’s business listings, traffic information and local search, while giving users a compelling reason to change a familiar habit.
Article Summary: Apple rolls out rebuilt India map with landmark-based directions, street-level imagery and labels in English and local languages. Lane guidance is intended to help drivers position themselves before a turn or an elevated road. Users can also plan journeys with up to 15 stops.

Article Title: MacKenzie Scott gave away $26 billion without asking for donations to be named after her, letting charities decide how to spend the money, while four wealthy donors put $189 million into democracy ins
Article Text:
Democracy programmes receive $369.2 million in major donations

The four wealthy donors behind $189 million in donations

MacKenzie Scott's different approach to philanthropy

Her donations extend beyond democracy programmes

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Democracy remains a small part of overall philanthropic giving

MacKenzie Scott has given away more than $26 billion since 2019, making her one of America's most prominent philanthropists. Her approach to charitable giving, however, differs from that of many wealthy donors. Rather than directing how recipients should use their money or seeking recognition through institutions named after her, Scott generally makes unrestricted donations, allowing organisations to decide where the funds are most needed. A different approach has emerged among some of America's biggest donors to democracy programmes. Four wealthy donor families have collectively contributed $189 million to university institutes carrying their names. A new investigation by The Chronicle of Philanthropy examines these contrasting approaches and the growing flow of private wealth into American democracy research and education.According to The Chronicle of Philanthropy, wealthy donors made 18 gifts worth at least $1 million each to democracy programmes between 2006 and 2025. These contributions amounted to a combined $369.2 million, with many of the publicly announced donations going to university institutes and centres focused on democracy, government and public policy.The funding increased considerably in recent years. Around $266.5 million, representing 72% of the total, was donated between 2021 and 2025. Contributions peaked in 2024, when democracy programmes received $84 million.Universities emerged as the biggest beneficiaries, receiving approximately four out of every five dollars donated during the period. Three of the gifts identified by the Chronicle went to other organisations, including the American Civil Liberties Union, Interfaith America and New York Historical.The four largest donations alone accounted for $189 million, with each going towards a university institute carrying the benefactors' names.The largest contribution came from Leonard Schaeffer and his late wife, Pamela, who donated $59 million to the University of Southern California in 2024. The money established the Leonard D. Schaeffer Institute for Public Policy & Government Service, a research and education centre headquartered at USC's Capital Campus in Washington, DC.Leonard Schaeffer founded health insurer WellPoint and is a professor of public policy at USC. He previously served as administrator of the Health Care Financing Administration during the administration of former US President Jimmy Carter. His name was already associated with the university through a 2009 donation that established the USC Schaeffer Center for Health Policy & Economics, which now houses the new institute.The second-largest contribution came from Francis and Kathleen Rooney, who donated $55 million to the University of Notre Dame in 2025 to endow the Rooney Democracy Institute. The institution was previously known as the Rooney Center for the Study of American Democracy, established in 2008 through the couple's foundation.Francis Rooney is a Republican who represented Florida's Fort Myers area in the US House of Representatives from 2017 to 2021. He previously served as CEO of investment and holding company Rooney Holdings Inc.The University of Virginia received $50 million from Bruce Karsh, co-founder of investment management firm Oaktree Capital Management, and his wife, Martha, in 2021. Both are alumni of the university's law school. Their contribution established the Karsh Institute of Democracy, with UVA announcing plans to match the donation.In 2022, the John Nau III Foundation contributed another $15 million to endow the institute, taking the university's total donations identified in the Chronicle's tally to $65 million, the highest among the recipients.The fourth major contribution came from Richard and Nancy Kinder, who donated $25 million to the University of Missouri in 2022 to expand the Kinder Institute on Constitutional Democracy. The latest contribution brought their total donations to the institute to approximately $60 million. Their foundation first endowed the institution in 2015. Richard Kinder is the co-founder of energy infrastructure company Kinder Morgan and earned his undergraduate and law degrees from the University of Missouri.Unlike donors who establish or expand institutions bearing their names, Scott generally gives organisations unrestricted funding, allowing them to determine how the money should be allocated.Her donations are made through Yield Giving, which identifies potential recipients through its own research and assessment process rather than relying exclusively on conventional grant applications. The organisations receiving the money are generally free to use it for their operational needs, programmes, staffing, infrastructure or other priorities.One example is Democracy Works, the nonprofit organisation behind TurboVote, a voter-engagement platform that helps Americans navigate voter registration and elections.In 2023, Democracy Works announced that it had received an unrestricted donation from Scott, describing it as the largest single contribution in the organisation's history. Its CEO, Luis Lozada, said the funding would provide a strong foundation for the organisation to continue innovating.The organisation did not have to establish an institute or programme carrying Scott's name in return for the donation. It was selected through Yield Giving's research process.Scott's approach is widely associated with trust-based philanthropy, which places greater responsibility on recipient organisations to decide how best to use the money rather than requiring donors to prescribe specific spending priorities.Scott's hands-off approach is not limited to organisations working on elections or democratic institutions. Her philanthropy spans education, healthcare, environmental protection, housing and other social causes.The Bob Woodruff Foundation, which supports military veterans, service members and their families, is another major recipient. Scott donated $15 million to the organisation in 2022, followed by another $20 million in 2025, bringing her contributions to $35 million.The foundation's CEO, Anne Marie Dougherty, has described Scott's approach as trust-based philanthropy.Education has also been a major focus of Scott's giving. She has donated more than $1 billion to Historically Black Colleges and Universities (HBCUs), supporting institutions that have historically faced funding disparities.Healthcare has similarly featured prominently in her philanthropic work. According to a Harvard Business School study cited by Fortune, healthcare was Yield Giving's largest category by absolute donation value in 2023.Despite the substantial contributions made by wealthy donors to democracy-focused institutions, the sector continues to account for a relatively small share of their overall philanthropy.The Chronicle's investigation found that education and healthcare remain major priorities for many wealthy donors, with democracy-related contributions representing only a portion of their charitable spending.
Article Summary: Democracy programmes receive $369.2 million in major donations. Four wealthy donor families have collectively contributed $189 million to university institutes carrying their names. MacKenzie Scott has given away more than $26 billion since 2019. Her approach to charitable giving differs from that of many wealthy donors.

Article Title: A UK woman paid £750 for an iPhone from Currys but received a dummy handset; after returning it twice and getting the same fake phone back, she recovered her money through her bank
Article Text:
Woman's £750 iPhone purchase turns into a repeated fake handset dispute

Customer finds two bags of rice instead of £3,300 MacBook

How criminals allegedly swapped expensive electronics before returning packages

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

What Currys said after customers reported fake iPhones and MacBooks replaced with rice

A customer ordering an expensive phone from a major electronics retailer would reasonably expect the package to contain the device she had paid for. As reported by the BBC, when a woman bought an iPhone for £750 from Currys in Carlisle, she found a dummy handset inside instead of an actual Apple phone. She contacted the retailer to arrange a return, hoping the issue would be resolved.After sending the package back, she received what appeared to be the same fake phone. When she tried the process again, the replacement was identical. She eventually recovered her money through her bank, while a BBC Watchdog investigation uncovered similar complaints involving other high-value electronics sold by the retailer.The customer, identified as Lucy in the BBC Watchdog investigation, had purchased an iPhone for £750 from Currys' Carlisle store. The package she received, however, did not contain the Apple smartphone she had ordered. Instead, there was a dummy handset inside.Lucy contacted Currys and attempted to return the item. The first return did not resolve the problem. When another handset was sent to her, she discovered that it was the same fake device she had already received.She tried returning it once more, only to find herself in the same position.Despite the repeated attempts to get the matter sorted, Currys declined to issue a refund. Lucy eventually turned to her bank and managed to recover the £750 payment. Her experience formed part of a wider investigation into customers who said the products delivered to them did not match what they had purchased.The investigation also heard from Andrew, who had spent £2,700 on an Apple MacBook. He had ordered a black model but received a silver laptop bearing marks left by old stickers. He suspected that the machine had previously been used and contacted Currys.The retailer asked him to return it. However, when a replacement arrived, Andrew took it to a Currys store and recorded the package being opened. The laptop inside was the very same machine he had sent back around three weeks earlier. His request for a refund was initially turned down.A subsequent check during the Watchdog investigation revealed that the laptop's warranty had been activated 19 days before Andrew purchased it. He later received a full refund, along with compensation.Another customer, Lee, had paid £3,300 for an Apple MacBook from Currys in Aldershot. Instead of finding a computer when he opened the package, he discovered two bags of rice. As reported by the BBC, he contacted Apple and was told that the device's 12-month warranty had already been activated 16 days before the purchase. Currys declined to reopen his complaint, but Lee eventually recovered the money through his bank. Currys is reimbursing the bank.The cases raised questions about how products could be returned to the retailer and subsequently reach other customers without the original contents being checked. The watchdog's investigation uncovered similar incidents in different parts of the UK, suggesting that the complaints could not simply be attributed to an isolated incident involving one individual.The programme examined the possibility of a retail fraud operation in which criminals replace expensive electronic products with cheaper items before returning the packages. High-value devices, including smartphones and laptops, are particularly attractive targets because the difference between the genuine product and its substitute can be substantial.In such cases, the original device is removed and something of little value is placed inside its packaging. If the returned parcel is not properly inspected, it can potentially enter the retailer's stock again and be sold to another customer. That creates a cycle in which an unsuspecting buyer pays the full price for a product that is no longer inside the box.When approached by Watchdog with the allegations, Currys said it served millions of customers through its stores and online business each year. The retailer described cases in which customers received an incorrect order as exceptionally rare and said it would investigate such incidents to make sure they were put right.The outcomes differed between the customers featured in the programme. Andrew received a full refund and compensation from Currys, while Lee obtained his money back through his bank, with the retailer agreeing to reimburse it. Lucy also recovered her £750 after approaching her bank, having been unable to secure a refund directly from Currys.
Article Summary: Customers reported fake iPhones and MacBooks replaced with rice. Currys said it served millions of customers through its stores and online business each year. The retailer described cases in which customers received an incorrect order as exceptionally rare and said it would investigate to make sure they were put right.

Article Title: As Nvidia founder Jensen Huang says, he is ready to come back as CEO; Nvidia interim CEO Colette Kress says board has determined it will not reinstate Huang and that is Board's ...
Article Text:
Background of Jensen Huang’s exit from Nvidia

Nvidia looks beyond leadership turmoil

Customers remain committed, says Colette Kress

Employee loyalty still remain strong

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Board draws a line under Jensen Huang's tenure

Nvidia’s board has decided not to reinstate co-founder Jensen Huang has the chief executive officer, Nvidia’s interim CEO Colette Kress said, signalling the AI chip giant intents to move ahead under its current leadership despite the recent departure of its longtime leader. Speaking to CNBC’s Jim Carter following Nvidia’s latest earnings report, Kress said that the board’s position on the future Huang at the company is clear. "Jensen resigned from his position with NVIDIA, and the board accepted his resignation," Kress said. "The board has determined that they will not reinstate Jensen. And that is our statement and what the board has decided to do." The comments come as speculation continues over whether Huang, who recently indicated he was prepared to return to the CEO role, could make a comeback at the company he co-founded.Huang stepped down as president, chief executive and board member with immediate effect, ending 33 years as CEO. Nvidia’s Form 8-K recorded the board’s acceptance and the appointments as of November 11, with Kress staying on as CFO while serving as interim CEO. The board is considering internal and external candidates for a permanent successor. The company also named Harvey C. Jones its first-ever board chair. The New York Times reported that Huang had an affair with an executive who reports to him.The reports surfaced shortly before the resignation was announced.Also Read| Nvidia Q3 results: Revenue jumps 103% to $115.8 billion; announces $0.25 per-share dividend Kress also addressed the concerns about the impact of the leadership shake-up and said that Nvidia’s priority now is to execute its growth strategy and serve its employees, customers and shareholders. "We wanna think about right now growing our business. We wanna grow in terms of everything that we need to do with our employees, our customers, our shareholders, and that is where we are gonna focus moving forward," she said.The remarks followed Nvidia's stronger-than-expected quarterly results and upgraded outlook. The company raised its fiscal 2028 revenue growth forecast to 75% from a previous estimate of 70%, helping ease investor concerns about the company's prospects after Huang's resignation.One of the main question which Nvidia is facing since the exit of Jensen Huang is that the major customers might shift more aggressively towards internally developed chips or rival suppliers such as AMD. However, Kress dismissed those conversations, saying that the demand for Nvidia’s AI computing platforms still remain robust. "[Hyperscalers] are the ones that are right now feverishly looking for more focus in terms of the compute that we have available," she said. "This concept that anything is changing in terms of any of our types of customers, that is just not true. They are all continuing to be with us, and we have a very deep breadth of different customers."As per Kress, many customers have also directly expressed their confidence in the company following the changes in the leadership. "I have seen already with many of these [customers] contacting me and saying, 'Great to see everything intact. Great to see that there's more supply. I need more demand.'"Apart from customer relationships, the exit of Jensen Huang from Nvidia has also raised questions about employee retention at the company whose culture and strategy were closely associated with its co-founder. Dress added that she is confident that Nvidia’s workforce is committed to the future of the company. "The company has been built under the perspective that the employees look at Nvidia as their life work, and many of them have been here for many decades, working with us both from a technology standpoint or a business and operations perspective," she said."We have high confidence that our employees are definitely still working, still working with us, and enjoy the work here at Nvidia."While Huang remains one of the most influential figures in the history of the semiconductor industry, Kress's comments make clear that Nvidia's board has no plans to reverse his resignation. Instead, the company is seeking to reassure investors, employees and customers that business momentum remains intact as it pursues continued growth in the artificial intelligence market, even without the executive who helped build Nvidia into the world's dominant AI chipmaker.
Article Summary: N Nvidia's interim CEO Colette Kress says the board has decided not to reinstate co-founder Jensen Huang as CEO. Kress said the company's priority now is to execute its growth strategy and serve its employees, customers and shareholders. The comments come as speculation continues over whether Huang, who recently indicated he was prepared to return to the CEO role, could make a comeback.

Article Title: Apple services down: Company confirms outage, as thousands of users report problems on App Store, Apple Music, AppleCare and iCloud Account and Sign In
Article Text:
Apple outage today has affected several services like iCloud, App Store, Apple Pay, Apple Support and Apple Music in the United States.

Apple services are hit across the world. The iPhone maker has confirmed outage. The company said that it is currently experiencing outages across multiple services. Apple Accounts, iCloud, the App Store, and Apple Music are all experiencing issues, with some users unable to sign in or access services. Company says this wasn’t a cyberattack.According to Apple's System Status page there are issues with iCloud’s Account & Sign In services affecting “all users,” which reportedly mean that it could make these service slow or unavailable. Just last week, a separate communications failure disrupted air traffic operations across the United States.On November 13, the Federal Aviation Administration issued its first nationwide ground stop in 25 years after it said a massive data traffic surge at two possible locations caused “instability with aircraft communications and radar feeds. ” Just a day earlier, a major Microsoft outage left users unable to access their Outlook email accounts or utilize core Microsoft 365 workplace tools, including Teams and Word. Article Summary: Outage affecting Apple services marks the latest in a string of high-profile technical disruptions to hit major financial, aviation, and technology infrastructure over the past two weeks. Article Title: Setback for Amazon, Google, Meta: US advances ban on Chinese data centre equipment amid national security fears
Article Text:
Data centre

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Why US is pushing forward and what it means for tech giants

The US government is moving forward with plans to block US imports of Chinese data center equipment, pushing past intense lobbying from major American tech giants including Amazon Google , and Meta, a report has said. Citing people briefed on the matter, news agency Reuters reported that at the center of the push is a US Federal Communications Commission (FCC) proposal, which was first reported by Reuters in August, to ban imports of new models of Chinese optical transceivers over national security concerns. These components are vital to modern data centers, allowing data to travel over fiber-optic cables at the speed of light.The report says that while opposition from Microsoft was already known, the resistance from Silicon Valley runs much deeper. Earlier this year, executives from Amazon, Google, Meta, CoreWeave and Cisco joined Microsoft in a meeting with White House officials to push back against the restriction. Citing two people briefed on the meeting, the report said that tech leaders warned that US companies could need up to a decade to comply with such a mandate.Although that lobbying initially cast doubt on whether the rule would survive, three additional sources familiar with the private deliberations confirmed that the administration is pressing ahead.The renewed momentum comes at a sensitive moment in Washington.Revelations surrounding Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy, alongside fresh scrutiny over cases of Nvidia AI chips being smuggled into China without Commerce Department intervention, have sparked louder demands from lawmakers for a tougher line on Chinese tech threats.For American cloud providers, replacing Chinese hardware is easier said than done. According to Counterpoint Research, China controls two-thirds of the global optical transceiver market. While American firms like Coherent and Lumentum make competing technology, a report from the Foundation for American Innovation notes they currently lack the manufacturing scale needed to replace Chinese suppliers.During talks with officials, US tech companies warned that Beijing could hit back by banning exports of indium phosphide, a critical mineral American manufacturers rely on to build their own optical transceivers.
Article Summary: The US government is moving forward with plans to block US imports of Chinese data center equipment, pushing past intense lobbying from major American tech giants. At the center of the push is a US Federal Communications Commission (FCC) proposal to ban imports of new models of Chinese optical transceivers over national security concerns.
